title: Clean and Unclean
lead: The Bible's system of ritual purity: states of being clean or unclean that decide who may come near the holy. Set out in Leviticus 11–15 and Numbers 19, it shapes the prophets' language of moral cleansing and the New Testament's debates over food, touch and Gentiles.

sections.b: The distinction between clean and unclean appears before Sinai, in Noah's ark (Genesis 7:2), and is set out as law in Leviticus 11–15 and Numbers 19, where contact with a corpse is the strongest source of uncleanness. The priests are to teach it (Ezekiel 44:23), and Haggai uses it as a parable: holiness does not pass to ordinary food by touch, but uncleanness does, so a people unclean in heart make their offerings unclean (Haggai 2:11–14). The prophets also turn the language into a picture of sin and forgiveness: "Wash, and be clean" (Isaiah 1:16), and God's promise to sprinkle clean water on his people (Ezekiel 36:25). In the Gospels Jesus touches the unclean and heals them, and his teaching that what goes into a person cannot defile (Mark 7:14–23) becomes, in Acts 10, a lesson about people: Gentiles are not to be called unclean.
